name: Rabshakeh
source_summary: Senior Assyrian official ('Rabshakeh' is his title, roughly 'chief officer' or 'field commander,' used here as his identifying name because Scripture records no personal name) sent by Sennacherib to besiege Jerusalem and demand its surrender, delivering a taunting speech in Hebrew designed to terrify the people and discredit their trust in the LORD.
family_friendly_summary: The Rabshakeh was a high-ranking officer in the army of Sennacherib, the king of Assyria. 'Rabshakeh' is actually his official title, not his personal name, but it's how the Bible identifies him since he isn't named otherwise. When the Assyrian army surrounded Jerusalem during King Hezekiah's reign, the Rabshakeh stood outside the city walls and shouted a long, frightening speech in Hebrew so the ordinary people could understand it -- mocking Judah's trust in Egypt for help, and especially mocking their trust in the LORD to save them. King Hezekiah's officials begged him to speak in a different language so the people wouldn't panic, but he refused and shouted his threats even louder. Hezekiah responded not with panic but with prayer, and God answered by destroying the Assyrian army that same night.
adult_story: The Rabshakeh -- an Assyrian title meaning something like 'chief officer' or 'field commander,' used here because Scripture never records this man's personal name -- was one of three senior officials King Sennacherib sent from Lachish, with a large army, to demand Jerusalem's surrender during Hezekiah's reign (2 Kings 18:17). Standing where the city's defenders could hear him, he delivered a long speech in Hebrew rather than Aramaic, deliberately aiming his words past Hezekiah's officials at the ordinary people on the wall (18:26-27). He mocked Judah's alliance with Egypt as 'a splintered reed,' and, most brazenly, claimed the LORD Himself had sent Assyria to destroy Jerusalem, so that trusting God to deliver the city was no different than trusting the false gods of every other nation Assyria had already conquered (18:19-25,33-35). Hezekiah's officials, horrified, begged him to speak in Aramaic so the common people wouldn't understand and lose heart, but he only raised his voice further (18:26-28). When Hezekiah heard the report, he tore his clothes, went to the temple, and sent to the prophet Isaiah for a word from God rather than answering the threat himself (19:1-5). The Rabshakeh later returned to find the Assyrian army had withdrawn to fight Libnah, and that same night the LORD's angel struck down 185,000 Assyrian soldiers, ending the threat entirely without a single blow from Judah (19:8,35-36). The Rabshakeh's blasphemous confidence, and its complete failure, stands as one of Scripture's clearest demonstrations that no human power's words can overrule God's own promises.

devotionals: The Rabshakeh mocked Judah's trust in the LORD and boasted no god could save them. That same night, God destroyed his army without a single blow from Judah.
No blasphemous boast can overrule what God has already promised. Jesus's power needs no help from human strength to accomplish His will.
